        "text": "\n\n\n**Identifying the Variable**\n\nI\u0027ve determined that \"G\" in the second equation ($r \u003d \\frac{G}{qB}$) represents the momentum (mv) of the charged particle.       "text": "\n\n\nIn this context, **$G$ stands for momentum** (in Slovenian: ***gibalna količina***). \n\nYou can see this by looking at the derivation from the first equation on the slide. The slide equates the magnetic force ($F_m \u003d qvB$) to the centripetal force ($F_c \u003d m\\frac{v^2}{r}$) required to keep the charge moving in a circle:\n\n$$q v B \u003d m \\frac{v^2}{r}$$\n\nIf you solve this equation for the radius $r$, you get:\n\n$$r \u003d \\frac{m v}{q B}$$\n\nSince momentum ($G$) is the product of mass and velocity ($G \u003d m v$), you can substitute it into the equation to get the final form shown on your slide:\n\n$$r \u003d \\frac{G}{q B}$$\n\n*(Note: While momentum is often denoted with the letter **$p$** in international literature, **$G$** is traditionally used in Slovenian physics textbooks, and the professor uses it here to mean $mv$.)*",
      "role": "model",
      "finishReason": "STOP",

      "text": "\n\n\nHere is the step-by-step logic and the formulas you need to solve the very first problem from the tutoring document (the one with the two hanging spheres).\n\n### The Problem\nTwo identical 1g spheres hang from 40 cm strings. They start with a total charge, but then one is discharged (razelektrimo). What happens? What was the initial charge $q_0$ if they end up 10 cm apart?\n\n---\n\n### Part 1: The Logic (What happens physically?)\n1. **The Attraction:** When one sphere is completely discharged, you have one charged sphere and one neutral sphere. The charged sphere will polarize the neutral one, causing them to attract and swing towards each other.\n2. **The Touch \u0026 Share:** Because they are identical conducting spheres, when they touch (\"se sprimeta\"), the charge from the charged sphere spreads evenly over both of them. \n   * **Formula:** $q_{final} \u003d \\frac{q_0 + 0}{2} \u003d \\frac{q_0}{2}$\n   * Now, *each* sphere has exactly half of the initial charge.\n3. **The Repulsion:** Since they now both have the exact same charge (same sign and magnitude), they repel each other and swing apart until they reach an equilibrium distance of $r \u003d 10 \\text{ cm}$.\n\n---\n\n### Part 2: Force Balance (The Equilibrium)\nOnce the spheres push apart and hang still, we just look at **one** of the spheres. There are three forces acting on it:\n1. **Gravity ($F_g$)** pulling straight down.\n2. **Electric Force ($F_e$)** pushing horizontally outward (Coulomb\u0027s Law).\n3. **Tension ($T$)** from the string pulling up and inward along the string.\n\nBecause the sphere isn\u0027t moving, the forces must balance out perfectly. If you draw the forces, they form a right triangle with the angle $\\alpha$ (the angle the string makes with the vertical axis).\n\nFrom the geometry of the forces, we get the balancing relationship:\n$$\\tan(\\alpha) \u003d \\frac{F_e}{F_g}$$\n\n---\n\n### Part 3: The Formulas to Recall\n\n**1. Coulomb\u0027s Law (Electric Force):**\n$$F_e \u003d \\frac{1}{4\\pi\\epsilon_0} \\frac{q_1 q_2}{r^2}$$\n*Since both spheres now have $q \u003d \\frac{q_0}{2}$, the formula becomes:*\n$$F_e \u003d \\frac{1}{4\\pi\\epsilon_0} \\frac{(q_0 / 2)^2}{r^2}$$\n*(Remember that $\\frac{1}{4\\pi\\epsilon_0} \\approx 9 \\times 10^9$)*\n\n**2. Gravity:**\n$$F_g \u003d m \\cdot g$$\n\n**3. Finding the Angle ($\\tan\\alpha$) from Geometry:**\nYou know the string length ($l \u003d 40 \\text{ cm}$) and the total distance between the spheres ($r \u003d 10 \\text{ cm}$).\nThe horizontal distance from the center line to one sphere is exactly half the distance: $x \u003d \\frac{r}{2} \u003d 5 \\text{ cm}$.\n* Use the Pythagorean theorem to find the vertical height $y$: \n  $y \u003d \\sqrt{l^2 - x^2}$\n* Then find $\\tan\\alpha$:\n  $$\\tan(\\alpha) \u003d \\frac{x}{y} \u003d \\frac{r/2}{\\sqrt{l^2 - (r/2)^2}}$$\n\n---\n\n### Part 4: How to solve it (Putting it together)\n1. Set the forces equal using the tangent ratio:\n   $$F_e \u003d m \\cdot g \\cdot \\tan(\\alpha)$$\n2. Plug in Coulomb\u0027s law for $F_e$:\n   $$\\frac{1}{4\\pi\\epsilon_0} \\frac{(q_0 / 2)^2}{r^2} \u003d m \\cdot g \\cdot \\tan(\\alpha)$$\n3. Isolate $(q_0 / 2)^2$:\n   $$(q_0 / 2)^2 \u003d r^2 \\cdot 4\\pi\\epsilon_0 \\cdot m \\cdot g \\cdot \\tan(\\alpha)$$\n4. Take the square root, and then multiply by 2 to get your final initial charge $q_0$.\n\n*(Just make sure you convert your mass to **kg** ($1\\text{ g} \u003d 10^{-3}\\text{ kg}$) and your distances to **meters** ($40\\text{ cm} \u003d 0.4\\text{ m}$, $10\\text{ cm} \u003d 0.1\\text{ m}$) before plugging them into the calculator!)*",

      "text": "\n\n\nHere is the step-by-step logic and the formulas you need to solve the **second problem** (the square plastic frame hanging between two charged plates).\n\n### The Problem\nA square frame (side $a \u003d 20\\text{ cm}$, mass $m \u003d 300\\text{ g}$, linear charge density $\\lambda \u003d +5\\ \\mu\\text{As/m}$) hangs from springs between two infinite charged planes. The top plane has $\\sigma_1 \u003d +10\\ \\mu\\text{As/m}^2$, and the bottom has $\\sigma_2 \u003d +20\\ \\mu\\text{As/m}^2$. How much do the springs stretch ($h$)?\n\n---\n\n### Part 1: The Logic (What happens physically?)\n1. **The Charge of the Frame:** We are given a linear charge density ($\\lambda$), which means charge per meter. To find the total charge ($q$) of the frame, we need to multiply this by the total length of the frame (the perimeter of the square).\n2. **The Electric Field:** The frame sits between two infinite planes.\n   * Both planes are positively charged, and the frame is positively charged. \n   * The **top plane** pushes the frame **down**.\n   * The **bottom plane** pushes the frame **up**. \n   * Because the bottom plane has a higher charge density ($\\sigma_2 \u003e \\sigma_1$), the *net* electric force will push the frame **upwards**.\n3. **The Equilibrium:** The frame is pulled down by gravity, but the electric field helps lift it up a little bit. The springs will stretch downwards just enough to support whatever weight is left over. \n   * Downward Forces \u003d Upward Forces\n\n---\n\n### Part 2: Force Balance (The Equilibrium)\nLet\u0027s list all the forces acting on the frame:\n*   **Downwards:** Gravity ($F_g$) + Electric force from top plane ($F_{e1}$)\n*   **Upwards:** Spring force ($F_{vz}$) + Electric force from bottom plane ($F_{e2}$)\n\nSo our balancing equation is:\n$$F_g + F_{e1} \u003d F_{vz} + F_{e2}$$\n\nIf we group the electric forces together to find the net electric force, we get:\n$$F_{vz} \u003d F_g - (F_{e2} - F_{e1})$$\n\n---\n\n### Part 3: The Formulas to Recall\n\n**1. Total Charge of the Square:**\n$$q \u003d \\lambda \\cdot L \u003d \\lambda \\cdot (4a)$$\n*(where $L$ is the perimeter of a square with side $a$)*\n\n**2. Electric Field of an Infinite Plane:**\n(From FIZIKA II slide 15 - neskončna ravnina)\n$$E \u003d \\frac{\\sigma}{2\\epsilon_0}$$\n\n**3. Electric Force:**\n$$F_e \u003d q \\cdot E$$\n*   Force from top plane: $F_{e1} \u003d q \\frac{\\sigma_1}{2\\epsilon_0}$\n*   Force from bottom plane: $F_{e2} \u003d q \\frac{\\sigma_2}{2\\epsilon_0}$\n\n**4. Gravity:**\n$$F_g \u003d m \\cdot g$$\n\n**5. Hooke\u0027s Law (Spring Force):**\n$$F_{vz} \u003d k_{tot} \\cdot h$$\n*(where $h$ is the stretch we are looking for. **See the pro-tip below regarding $k_{tot}$!**)*\n\n---\n\n### Part 4: How to solve it (Putting it together)\n1. Substitute all your formulas into the balance equation:\n   $$k_{tot} \\cdot h \u003d m \\cdot g - \\left( q \\frac{\\sigma_2}{2\\epsilon_0} - q \\frac{\\sigma_1}{2\\epsilon_0} \\right)$$\n2. Factor out the common terms for the electric force to make it cleaner:\n   $$k_{tot} \\cdot h \u003d m \\cdot g - \\frac{q}{2\\epsilon_0}(\\sigma_2 - \\sigma_1)$$\n3. Isolate $h$:\n   $$h \u003d \\frac{m \\cdot g - \\frac{\\lambda \\cdot 4a}{2\\epsilon_0}(\\sigma_2 - \\sigma_1)}{k_{tot}}$$\n\n***\n\n### 🚨 Pro-Tip for this specific problem (Watch out for $k$!):\nThe problem states \"sta nameščeni dve vzmeti ($k\u003d70\\text{ N/m}$)\". \nNormally, if you have two springs parallel to each other, the total spring constant is $k_{tot} \u003d 2k \u003d 140\\text{ N/m}$. \n\nHowever, if you actually calculate the numbers:\n* $F_g \u003d 0.3 \\cdot 9.81 \u003d 2.943\\text{ N}$\n* $F_{e(net)} \u003d \\frac{4 \\cdot 0.2 \\cdot 5\\times 10^{-6}}{2 \\cdot 8.85\\times 10^{-12}} (20\\times 10^{-6} - 10\\times 10^{-6}) \\approx 2.259\\text{ N}$\n* Net force to be held by springs \u003d $2.943 - 2.259 \u003d \\mathbf{0.684\\text{ N}}$\n\nIf you divide this by **$70$**, you get exactly **$0.00977\\text{ m}$ (or $9.8\\text{ mm}$)**, which matches the provided solution! \n\n**Conclusion:** The author of the problem either meant that the *combined* stiffness of the system is $k_{tot} \u003d 70\\text{ N/m}$, OR they made a mistake and forgot to multiply by 2.       "text": "\n\n\nMoving sequentially down the page, the **third problem** is the first one inside the \"1. Kolokvij\" box (with the small sphere hanging between a large sphere and a vertical plane). \n\nHere is the step-by-step logic and the formulas for this problem.\n\n### The Problem\nA small mass ($m \u003d 10\\text{ g}$) with a negative charge ($q \u003d -0.5\\ \\mu\\text{As}$) hangs from a string ($l \u003d 75\\text{ cm}$) between a large non-conducting sphere (radius $R \u003d 25\\text{ cm}$) and an infinite vertical plane ($\\sigma_2 \u003d +10\\ \\mu\\text{As/m}^2$). The string anchor is at a distance $a \u003d 50\\text{ cm}$ from the plane and $a \u003d 50\\text{ cm}$ from the *surface* of the sphere. \nThe small sphere swings to the left and stops at a distance $d \u003d 10\\text{ cm}$ from the large sphere\u0027s surface. What is the surface charge density ($\\sigma_1$) of the large sphere?\n\n---\n\n### Part 1: The Logic (What happens physically?)\n1. **The Attractions:** The small sphere has a **negative** charge. The plane on the right has a **positive** charge (+10), so it attracts the small sphere to the right. However, the problem states the sphere swings to the **left**. This means the large sphere must also be **positively** charged, and its attractive pull must be stronger than the plane\u0027s pull.\n2. **The Geometry (The tricky part!):** Look very closely at the dashed lines for \"$a$\" in the diagram. The line for $a$ goes from the anchor to the **surface** of the large sphere, not the center. \n   * When the small sphere swings to the left and stops at distance $d$ from the surface, it has moved horizontally by exactly $x \u003d a - d \u003d 50 - 10 \u003d \\mathbf{40\\text{ cm}}$ from its starting point.\n   * It is now at a total distance of $r \u003d R + d \u003d 25 + 10 \u003d \\mathbf{35\\text{ cm}}$ from the *center* of the large sphere.\n3. **The Equilibrium:** The small sphere is pulled down by gravity, pulled up/inward by the string\u0027s tension, pulled right by the plane, and pulled left by the large sphere. Since it\u0027s standing still, all these forces balance out.\n\n---\n\n### Part 2: Force Balance (The Equilibrium)\nWe look at the horizontal and vertical forces separately, just like in the first problem:\n*   **Vertical:** The vertical part of the string\u0027s tension holds up gravity: $T \\cos\\alpha \u003d F_g$\n*   **Horizontal:** The horizontal part of the tension pulls to the right to balance out the net electric force pulling to the left: $T \\sin\\alpha \u003d F_{e1} - F_{e2}$\n\nDividing the horizontal equation by the vertical one gives us our master balance equation:\n$$\\tan\\alpha \u003d \\frac{F_{e1} - F_{e2}}{F_g}$$\nWhich rearranges to:\n$$F_{e1} - F_{e2} \u003d m \\cdot g \\cdot \\tan\\alpha$$\n\n---\n\n### Part 3: The Formulas to Recall\n\n**1. Electric Field \u0026 Force of an Infinite Plane:**\n$$E_2 \u003d \\frac{\\sigma_2}{2\\epsilon_0} \\implies F_{e2} \u003d |q| \\frac{\\sigma_2}{2\\epsilon_0}$$\n\n**2. Electric Field \u0026 Force of a Charged Sphere:**\n(By Gauss\u0027s law, outside the sphere, it acts like a point charge at its center. The total charge is $Q \u003d \\sigma_1 \\cdot 4\\pi R^2$).\n$$E_1 \u003d \\frac{1}{4\\pi\\epsilon_0} \\frac{Q}{r^2} \u003d \\frac{1}{4\\pi\\epsilon_0} \\frac{\\sigma_1 4\\pi R^2}{(R+d)^2} \u003d \\frac{\\sigma_1 R^2}{\\epsilon_0 (R+d)^2}$$\n$$F_{e1} \u003d |q| \\frac{\\sigma_1 R^2}{\\epsilon_0 (R+d)^2}$$\n\n**3. Finding the Angle ($\\tan\\alpha$) from Geometry:**\nUsing the horizontal displacement $x \u003d a - d \u003d 40\\text{ cm}$ and string length $l \u003d 75\\text{ cm}$:\n*   Find the vertical drop $y$ using Pythagorean theorem: $y \u003d \\sqrt{l^2 - x^2}$\n*   $$\\tan\\alpha \u003d \\frac{x}{y} \u003d \\frac{a - d}{\\sqrt{l^2 - (a - d)^2}}$$\n\n---\n\n### Part 4: How to solve it (Putting it together)\n1. Substitute the force formulas into the balance equation:\n   $$|q| \\frac{\\sigma_1 R^2}{\\epsilon_0 (R+d)^2} - |q| \\frac{\\sigma_2}{2\\epsilon_0} \u003d m \\cdot g \\cdot \\tan\\alpha$$\n2. Divide the whole equation by $|q|$ and multiply by $\\epsilon_0$ to start isolating $\\sigma_1$:\n   $$\\frac{\\sigma_1 R^2}{(R+d)^2} - \\frac{\\sigma_2}{2} \u003d \\frac{m \\cdot g \\cdot \\epsilon_0 \\cdot \\tan\\alpha}{|q|}$$\n3. Move $\\frac{\\sigma_2}{2}$ to the other side:\n   $$\\frac{\\sigma_1 R^2}{(R+d)^2} \u003d \\frac{\\sigma_2}{2} + \\frac{m \\cdot g \\cdot \\epsilon_0 \\cdot \\tan\\alpha}{|q|}$$\n4.         "text": " sequentially down the page, the **third problem** is the first one inside the \"1. Kolokvij\" box (with"

        "text": " the small sphere hanging between a large sphere and a vertical plane). \n\nHere is the step-by-step logic"
      }, {
        "text": " and the formulas for this problem.\n\n### The Problem\nA small mass ($m \u003d 10\\text{"
      }, {
        "text": " g}$) with a negative charge ($q \u003d -0.5\\ \\mu\\text{As}$) hangs from a string ($l \u003d 75"
      }, {
        "text": "\\text{ cm}$) between a large non-conducting sphere (radius $R \u003d 25\\text{ cm}$) and an infinite vertical"
      }, {
        "text": " plane ($\\sigma_2 \u003d +10\\ \\mu\\text{As/m}^2$). The string anchor"
      }, {
        "text": " is at a distance $a \u003d 50\\text{ cm}$ from the plane and $a \u003d 50\\text{"
      }, {
        "text": " cm}$ from the *surface* of the sphere. \nThe small sphere swings to the left and stops at a distance $d \u003d"
      }, {
        "text": " 10\\text{ cm}$ from the large sphere\u0027s surface. What is the surface charge density ($\\sigma_1$) of the large sphere"
      }, {
        "text": "?\n\n---\n\n### Part 1: The Logic (What happens physically?)\n1. **The Attractions:** The small sphere"
      }, {
        "text": " has a **negative** charge. The plane on the right has a **positive** charge (+10), so it attracts the small sphere to the"
      }, {
        "text": " right. However, the problem states the sphere swings to the **left**. This means the large sphere must also be **positively** charged, and its"
      }, {
        "text": " attractive pull must be stronger than the plane\u0027s pull.\n2. **The Geometry (The tricky part!):** Look very"
      }, {
        "text": " closely at the dashed lines for \"$a$\" in the diagram. The line for $a$ goes from the anchor to the **surface** of the large"
      }, {
        "text": " sphere, not the center. \n   * When the small sphere swings to the left and stops at distance $d$ from the surface,"
      }, {
        "text": " it has moved horizontally by exactly $x \u003d a - d \u003d 50 - 10 \u003d \\mathbf{40\\text{"
      }, {
        "text": " cm}}$ from its starting point.\n   * It is now at a total distance of $r \u003d R + d \u003d"
      }, {
        "text": " 25 + 10 \u003d \\mathbf{35\\text{ cm}}$ from the *center* of the large sphere."
      }, {
        "text": "\n3. **The Equilibrium:** The small sphere is pulled down by gravity, pulled up/inward by the string\u0027"
      }, {
        "text": "s tension, pulled right by the plane, and pulled left by the large sphere. Since it\u0027s standing still, all"
      }, {
        "text": " these forces balance out.\n\n---\n\n### Part 2: Force Balance (The Equilibrium)\nWe look at the horizontal and"
      }, {
        "text": " vertical forces separately, just like in the first problem:\n*   **Vertical:** The vertical part of the string\u0027"
      }, {
        "text": "s tension holds up gravity: $T \\cos\\alpha \u003d F_g$\n*   **Horizontal:** The horizontal part"
      }, {
        "text": " of the tension pulls to the right to balance out the net electric force pulling to the left: $T \\sin\\alpha \u003d"
      }, {
        "text": " F_{e1} - F_{e2}$\n\nDividing the horizontal equation by the vertical one gives us our"
      }, {
        "text": " master balance equation:\n$$\\tan\\alpha \u003d \\frac{F_{e1} - F_{e2}}{"
      }, {
        "text": "F_g}$$\nWhich rearranges to:\n$$F_{e1} - F_{e2} \u003d m \\cdot g \\cdot \\"
      }, {
        "text": "tan\\alpha$$\n\n---\n\n### Part 3: The Formulas to Recall\n\n**1. Electric Field \u0026 Force of an Infinite Plane:**\n$$"
      }, {
        "text": "E_2 \u003d \\frac{\\sigma_2}{2\\epsilon_0} \\implies F_{e2} \u003d |q"
      }, {
        "text": "| \\frac{\\sigma_2}{2\\epsilon_0}$$\n\n**2. Electric Field \u0026 Force of a"
      }, {
        "text": " Charged Sphere:**\n(By Gauss\u0027s law, outside the sphere, it acts like a point charge at its center. The total charge is"
      }, {
        "text": " $Q \u003d \\sigma_1 \\cdot 4\\pi R^2$).\n$$E_1 \u003d \\"
      }, {
        "text": "frac{1}{4\\pi\\epsilon_0} \\frac{Q}{r^2} \u003d \\frac"
      }, {
        "text": "{1}{4\\pi\\epsilon_0} \\frac{\\sigma_1 4\\pi R^2"
      }, {
        "text": "}{(R+d)^2} \u003d \\frac{\\sigma_1 R^2}{\\epsilon_0 (R+d)^2}$$\n$$F"
      }, {
        "text": "_{e1} \u003d |q| \\frac{\\sigma_1 R^2}{\\epsilon_0 (R+"
      }, {
        "text": "d)^2}$$\n\n**3. Finding the Angle ($\\tan\\alpha$) from Geometry:**\nUsing the horizontal displacement"
      }, {
        "text": " $x \u003d a - d \u003d 40\\text{ cm}$ and string length $l \u003d 75\\text{ cm"
      }, {
        "text": "}$:\n*   Find the vertical drop $y$ using Pythagorean theorem: $y \u003d \\sqrt{l^2 - x^2}$"
      }, {
        "text": "\n*   $$\\tan\\alpha \u003d \\frac{x}{y} \u003d \\frac{a - d}{\\sqrt{l^2 - ("
      }, {
        "text": "a - d)^2}}$$\n\n---\n\n### Part 4: How to solve it (Putting it together)"
      }, {
        "text": "\n1. Substitute the force formulas into the balance equation:\n   $$|q| \\frac{\\sigma_1 R^2}{\\epsilon_"
      }, {

      }, {
        "text": "} \u003d m \\cdot g \\cdot \\tan\\alpha$$\n2. Divide the whole equation by $|q|$"
      }, {
        "text": " and multiply by $\\epsilon_0$ to start isolating $\\sigma_1$:\n   $$\\frac{\\sigma_1 R^"
      }, {
        "text": "2}{(R+d)^2} - \\frac{\\sigma_2}{2} \u003d \\frac{m \\"
      }, {
        "text": "cdot g \\cdot \\epsilon_0 \\cdot \\tan\\alpha}{|q|}$$\n3. Move $\\frac"
      }, {
        "text": "{\\sigma_2}{2}$ to the other side:\n   $$\\frac{\\sigma_1 R^2}{("
      }, {
        "text": "R+d)^2} \u003d \\frac{\\sigma_2}{2} + \\frac{m \\cdot g"
      }, {
        "text": " \\cdot \\epsilon_0 \\cdot \\tan\\alpha}{|q|}$$\n4. Multiply by the inverted radius"

      "text": "\n\n\n\nMoving on to the **fourth problem**! This is the one near the middle of page 1, right below the previous problem. \n\nThis is a fantastic problem because it tests two completely different physics concepts: **Force** (to figure out the direction) and **Conservation of Energy** (to figure out the speed).\n\n### The Problem\nWe have two non-conducting spheres separated by $d \u003d 2\\text{ m}$ (center-to-center).\n*   **Sphere 1:** radius $r_1 \u003d 3\\text{ cm}$, charge $q_1 \u003d +5\\ \\mu\\text{As}$\n*   **Sphere 2:** radius $r_2 \u003d 5\\text{ cm}$, charge $q_2 \u003d +10\\ \\mu\\text{As}$\nA small sphere ($m \u003d 1\\text{ g}$, $q \u003d -0.5\\ \\mu\\text{As}$) is placed between them, at a distance $a \u003d 75\\text{ cm}$ from the center of Sphere 1. \n**Questions:** Which sphere does it fly towards? What is its speed right before it hits the surface?\n\n---\n\n### Part 1: The Logic (Which way does it fly?)\nThe small sphere has a **negative** charge. Both large spheres are **positively** charged. Therefore, the small sphere is being pulled to the left by Sphere 1 and to the right by Sphere 2.\n*   To find out which way it goes, we simply calculate the electric force from both spheres at the starting position and see which one is bigger!\n*   It starts at distance $a$ from Sphere 1, which means it is at distance $(d - a)$ from Sphere 2.\n\n### Part 2: The Logic (Finding the speed)\nOnce we know it flies towards Sphere 1, it will accelerate. However, as it gets closer to Sphere 1, the force pulling it gets stronger and stronger. Because the **force is not constant, you cannot use basic kinematics ($F\u003dma$)**. \n*   Whenever a force changes with distance, you must use **Conservation of Energy**.\n*   The electric field does work on the small sphere. Its **Electric Potential Energy** decreases, and its **Kinetic Energy** increases. \n*   We need to calculate the *Electric Potential ($V$)* at the starting point, and the *Electric Potential* at the end point (right as it touches the surface of Sphere 1).\n\n---\n\n### Part 3: The Formulas to Recall\n\n**1. Coulomb\u0027s Law (To find direction):**\n$$F \u003d \\frac{1}{4\\pi\\epsilon_0} \\frac{|q_a| |q_b|}{r^2}$$\n*(Remember: $F_1$ uses distance $a$, and $F_2$ uses distance $d-a$)*\n\n**2. Electric Potential ($V$) of a Sphere:**\n(From FIZIKA II slide 23, the potential of a point charge/sphere)\n$$V \u003d \\frac{1}{4\\pi\\epsilon_0} \\frac{Q}{r}$$\n*Because there are two spheres, the total potential at any point in space is simply the sum of the potentials from both spheres:*\n$$V_{total} \u003d V_1 + V_2 \u003d \\frac{1}{4\\pi\\epsilon_0} \\left( \\frac{q_1}{r_{from\\_1}} + \\frac{q_2}{r_{from\\_2}} \\right)$$\n\n**3. Conservation of Energy:**\nThe change in kinetic energy equals the negative change in potential energy:\n$$E_k \u003d W_{electric}$$\n$$\\frac{1}{2}mv^2 \u003d q \\cdot (V_{start} - V_{end})$$\n*(Note: $q$ here is the charge of the **small moving sphere**, and you MUST include its negative sign in the calculation!)*\n\n---\n\n### Part 4: How to solve it (Putting it together)\n\n**Step 1: Prove the direction**\nCalculate $F_1$ (pulling left) and $F_2$ (pulling right):\n*   $F_1 \u003d \\frac{1}{4\\pi\\epsilon_0} \\frac{|q| \\cdot q_1}{a^2}$\n*   $F_2 \u003d \\frac{1}{4\\pi\\epsilon_0} \\frac{|q| \\cdot q_2}{(d-a)^2}$\n*(When you plug in the numbers, you will find $F_1 \u003e F_2$, proving it flies towards Sphere 1.)*\n\n**Step 2: Find the Initial Potential ($V_{start}$)**\nAt the starting point, it is $0.75\\text{ m}$ from Sphere 1 and $1.25\\text{ m}$ from Sphere 2:\n$$V_{start} \u003d \\frac{1}{4\\pi\\epsilon_0} \\left( \\frac{q_1}{0.75} + \\frac{q_2}{1.25} \\right)$$\n\n**Step 3: Find the Final Potential ($V_{end}$)**\nIt stops exactly when it hits the *surface* of Sphere 1. At this moment, it is $r_1 \u003d 0.03\\text{ m}$ away from the center of Sphere 1. \nIts distance to Sphere 2 is now $(d - r_1) \u003d 1.97\\text{ m}$:\n$$V_{end} \u003d \\frac{1}{4\\pi\\epsilon_0} \\left( \\frac{q_1}{0.03} + \\frac{q_2}{1.97} \\right)$$\n\n**Step 4: Solve for Velocity**\nUse the energy conservation formula. Because $V_{end}$ is much larger than $V_{start}$, the term $(V_{start} - V_{end})$ will be negative. But since the small charge $q$ is *also* negative, the whole right side becomes positive, which makes sense because kinetic energy must be positive!\n$$\\frac{1}{2} m v^2 \u003d q \\cdot (V_{start} - V_{end})$$\n$$v \u003d \\sqrt{ \\frac{2 \\cdot q \\cdot (V_{start} - V_{end})}{m} }$$\n\n*(Make sure you convert the mass to kg ($0.001\\text{ kg}$) and the charges to Coulombs ($10^{-6}\\text{ C}$). You will get exactly $v \u003d 37.6\\text{ m/s}$!)*",

      "text": "\n\n\nHere is the step-by-step logic and the formulas you need for the **fifth problem** (the one at the very bottom of page 1, with the hanging metal rod and the long straight wire). \n\nThis is your first **Magnetism** problem! It perfectly combines the pendulum mechanics from the previous problems with the magnetic force between two wires.\n\n### The Problem\nA metal rod (length $L \u003d 50\\text{ cm}$, mass $M \u003d 5\\text{ g}$) hangs from two strings (length $l \u003d 50.1\\text{ cm}$). A current $I_1 \u003d 12\\text{ A}$ flows through it. \nA long straight wire runs parallel to it, located $b\u003d50\\text{ cm}$ below the ceiling and starting at a horizontal distance $a \u003d 5\\text{ cm}$ from the resting rod. \nThe rod swings sideways and goes **up** by $h \u003d 1\\text{ mm}$ until it is at the exact same height as the long wire.\n*   **a)** What is the current $I_2$ in the long wire if it swings *towards* it?\n*   **b)** What must $I_2$ be to make the rod swing the exact same amount in the *opposite* direction?\n\n---\n\n### Part 1: The Logic (What happens physically?)\n1. **The Magnetic Force:** When you have two parallel wires carrying current, they create magnetic fields that push or pull on each other.\n   * If the currents flow in the **same direction**, they **attract**.\n   * If the currents flow in **opposite directions**, they **repel**.\n2. **The Pendulum Swing (The tricky geometry!):**\n   * The strings are $l \u003d 50.1\\text{ cm}$ long, so the rod naturally hangs $50.1\\text{ cm}$ below the ceiling. \n   * It swings until it goes up by $1\\text{ mm}$ ($0.1\\text{ cm}$). Its new depth is exactly $50.1 - 0.1 \u003d \\mathbf{50.0\\text{ cm}}$. \n   * Notice that $50.0\\text{ cm}$ is exactly the depth $b$ of the long wire! So they are now perfectly level horizontally.\n   * By swinging up, it also moved horizontally. We must calculate this horizontal swing ($x$) using a right triangle to find out exactly how close (or far) it is from the long wire now.\n3. **The Equilibrium:** Just like the electrostatic problems, gravity pulls down, tension pulls up/in, and the magnetic force pulls horizontally. \n\n---\n\n### Part 2: The Geometry (Finding distance $d$)\nBefore calculating forces, we need the distance between the rod and the wire. Let\u0027s find the horizontal swing distance ($x$):\n*   Hypotenuse (string length) \u003d $l \u003d 50.1\\text{ cm}$\n*   Vertical side (new depth) \u003d $y \u003d 50.0\\text{ cm}$\n*   Horizontal side (swing) \u003d $x \u003d \\sqrt{l^2 - y^2} \u003d \\sqrt{50.1^2 - 50.0^2} \\approx \\mathbf{3.164\\text{ cm}}$\n\n**For Part a) (Attraction):** The rod swings *towards* the wire. It started $a \u003d 5\\text{ cm}$ away, and swung $3.164\\text{ cm}$ closer. \n*   Distance $d \u003d 5 - 3.164 \u003d \\mathbf{1.836\\text{ cm}}$\n\n**For Part b) (Repulsion):** The rod swings *away* from the wire by the same amount. \n*   Distance $d \u003d 5 + 3.164 \u003d \\mathbf{8.164\\text{ cm}}$\n\n---\n\n### Part 3: The Formulas to Recall\n\n**1. Magnetic Field of a Long Straight Wire:**\n(From FIZIKA II slide 63)\n$$B \u003d \\frac{\\mu_0 I_2}{2\\pi d}$$\n\n**2. Magnetic Force on a Wire (The Rod):**\n(From FIZIKA II slide 57)\n$$F_m \u003d I_1 L B$$\n*Combining these two gives the famous formula for the force between two parallel wires:*\n$$F_m \u003d \\frac{\\mu_0 I_1 I_2 L}{2\\pi d}$$\n\n**3. Force Balance (from the pendulum triangle):**\nJust like in problem 3, the ratio of the horizontal force to the vertical force is the same as the ratio of the horizontal distance to the vertical distance:\n$$\\frac{F_m}{F_g} \u003d \\frac{x}{y}$$\n$$F_m \u003d M \\cdot g \\cdot \\frac{x}{y}$$\n\n*(⚠️ **Warning:** Do not confuse $L$ with $l$! $L \u003d 50\\text{ cm}$ is the length of the metal rod feeling the magnetic force. $l \u003d 50.1\\text{ cm}$ is the length of the string holding it up.)*\n\n---\n\n### Part 4: How to solve it (Putting it together)\n\n**Step 1: Calculate the required Magnetic Force**\nSince the geometry of the swing is identical for both Part a and Part b (it swings by $x\u003d3.164\\text{ cm}$ and $y\u003d50.0\\text{ cm}$ in both cases), the required force is the same for both!\n$$F_m \u003d 0.005\\text{ kg} \\cdot 9.81\\text{ m/s}^2 \\cdot \\frac{3.164}{50.0} \\approx \\mathbf{0.003104\\text{ N}}$$\n\n**Step 2: Solve for $I_2$ in Part a)**\nSet the required force equal to the magnetic force formula:\n$$0.003104 \u003d \\frac{\\mu_0 \\cdot I_1 \\cdot I_2 \\cdot L}{2\\pi \\cdot d}$$\nIsolate $I_2$:\n$$I_2 \u003d \\frac{0.003104 \\cdot 2\\pi \\cdot d}{\\mu_0 \\cdot I_1 \\cdot L}$$\n*(Plug in $\\mu_0 \u003d 4\\pi \\times 10^{-7}$, $I_1 \u003d 12$, $L \u003d 0.5$, and **$d \u003d 0.01836\\text{ m}$**. The $\\pi$ cancels out nicely. You will get **$I_2 \\approx 47.5\\text{ A}$**)*\n\n**Step 3: Solve for $I_2$ in Part b)**\nUse the exact same isolated formula, but plug in the *repulsive* distance **$d \u003d 0.08164\\text{ m}$**.\nBecause the distance is much larger, the magnetic field is weaker, meaning you need a much massive current to achieve the same force!\n*(Plug it in, and you will get **$I_2 \\approx 211.1\\text{ A}$**. The direction of this current must be **opposite** to $I_1$ to create repulsion.)*",

      "text": "\n\n\nHere is the step-by-step logic and formulas for the **sixth problem** (the first problem at the top of Page 2, with the two large spheres and the small charge $q_3$ placed between them).\n\nThis is a great problem because it is a two-part question: the first part is pure **Electrostatics (Force balance)**, and the second part is exactly like Problem 4, using **Conservation of Energy**.\n\n### The Problem\nWe have two large spheres separated by $a \u003d 1\\text{ m}$ (center-to-center).\n*   **Left Sphere 1:** $Q_1 \u003d +2\\ \\mu\\text{As}$, radius $R \u003d 5\\text{ cm}$\n*   **Right Sphere 2:** $Q_2 \u003d +3\\ \\mu\\text{As}$, radius $R \u003d 5\\text{ cm}$\nA small negative charge ($q_3 \u003d -0.3\\ \\mu\\text{As}$, $m \u003d 10\\text{ g}$) is placed between them.\n*   **Part A:** Where must we place $q_3$ so the net force on it is zero ($x \u003d ?$)?\n*   **Part B:** If we place it there, but then suddenly remove the left sphere ($Q_1$), with what speed does $q_3$ crash into the right sphere ($Q_2$)?\n\n---\n\n### Part 1: The Logic (Finding the zero-force point)\nThe small charge $q_3$ is negative, so it is attracted to **both** of the large positive spheres. \nFor it to stay perfectly still (zero net force), the pull to the left ($F_1$) must exactly equal the pull to the right ($F_2$). \nBecause $Q_2$ has a stronger charge than $Q_1$, the small charge will need to be placed **closer to $Q_1$** for the forces to balance out.\n\n### Part 2: The Logic (Finding the crash speed)\nOnce we find the starting position $x$, the problem says we take the left sphere ($Q_1$) far away. This means $Q_1$ **no longer exists** in our calculation.\nNow, $q_3$ only feels the pull from $Q_2$, so it accelerates to the right. Just like in problem 4, because the electric force gets stronger as it gets closer, we **cannot use $F\u003dma$**. We must use **Conservation of Energy**:\n*   The Electric Potential Energy of the system decreases, converting into Kinetic Energy.\n*   We need the Electric Potential ($V$) created by $Q_2$ at the starting point, and the potential at the surface of $Q_2$.\n\n---\n\n### Part 3: The Formulas to Recall\n\n**1. Coulomb\u0027s Law (To balance forces):**\n$$F \u003d \\frac{1}{4\\pi\\epsilon_0} \\frac{|q_a| |q_b|}{r^2}$$\n\n**2. Electric Potential ($V$) of a Point/Sphere:**\n$$V \u003d \\frac{1}{4\\pi\\epsilon_0} \\frac{Q}{r}$$\n\n**3. Conservation of Energy:**\n$$\\frac{1}{2}mv^2 \u003d q_3 \\cdot (V_{start} - V_{end})$$\n*(Remember, $q_3$ is negative, and since $V_{end}$ will be larger than $V_{start}$, the subtraction will also be negative, making the whole right side positive!)*\n\n---\n\n### Part 4: How to solve it (Putting it together)\n\n**Step 1: Balance the forces to find $x$**\nLet $x$ be the distance from $Q_1$. That means the distance from $Q_2$ is $(a - x)$.\n$$F_1 \u003d F_2$$\n$$\\frac{1}{4\\pi\\epsilon_0} \\frac{|q_3| Q_1}{x^2} \u003d \\frac{1}{4\\pi\\epsilon_0} \\frac{|q_3| Q_2}{(a - x)^2}$$\n*Notice that $\\frac{1}{4\\pi\\epsilon_0}$ AND $|q_3|$ cancel out completely! The equilibrium position doesn\u0027t even depend on the small charge.*\n$$\\frac{Q_1}{x^2} \u003d \\frac{Q_2}{(a - x)^2}$$\nTake the square root of both sides to make it easy:\n$$\\frac{\\sqrt{Q_1}}{x} \u003d \\frac{\\sqrt{Q_2}}{a - x}$$\nCross-multiply and solve for $x$:\n$$x \u003d a \\frac{\\sqrt{Q_1}}{\\sqrt{Q_1} + \\sqrt{Q_2}}$$\n*(Plug in $a\u003d1$, $Q_1\u003d2$, and $Q_2\u003d3$. You will get **$x \u003d 0.449\\text{ m}$ (or $45\\text{ cm}$)**. This perfectly matches the solution!)*\n\n**Step 2: Find Initial Potential ($V_{start}$)**\nNow, $Q_1$ is gone. We only care about the potential from $Q_2$. The distance to $Q_2$ is $(a - x) \u003d 1 - 0.45 \u003d 0.55\\text{ m}$.\n$$V_{start} \u003d \\frac{1}{4\\pi\\epsilon_0} \\frac{Q_2}{0.55}$$\n\n**Step 3: Find Final Potential ($V_{end}$)**\nIt crashes into the surface of $Q_2$, meaning it is now $R \u003d 5\\text{ cm} \u003d 0.05\\text{ m}$ away from the center of $Q_2$.\n$$V_{end} \u003d \\frac{1}{4\\pi\\epsilon_0} \\frac{Q_2}{0.05}$$\n\n**Step 4: Solve for Velocity**\nUse the energy conservation formula:\n$$\\frac{1}{2} m v^2 \u003d q_3 \\cdot (V_{start} - V_{end})$$\n$$v \u003d \\sqrt{ \\frac{2 \\cdot q_3 \\cdot (V_{start} - V_{end})}{m} }$$\n\n*(Make sure to convert $m \u003d 0.01\\text{ kg}$ and $q_3 \u003d -0.3 \\times 10^{-6}\\text{ C}$.)* \n\n***\n\n### 🚨 A Note on the Final Answer for Velocity:\nIf you do the math perfectly with no rounding, you will get $v \\approx \\mathbf{5.42 \\text{ m/s}}$. \nThe provided solution says **$5.24 \\text{ m/s}$**. \nIn physics classes, it is incredibly common for professors or TAs to make a slight \"dyslexia\" typo when typing the answer key (swapping the 4 and the 2). Do not let it drive you crazy if your calculator says $5.42$ instead of $5.24$; your physics and logic are 100% correct!",

      "text": "\n\n\nHere is the step-by-step logic and the formulas you need for the **seventh problem** (the second one on Page 2, with the three charges in an equilateral triangle).\n\nThis is a beautiful problem because it tests **Vector Addition of Forces** (for Part A) and **Conservation of Energy** (for Part B).\n\n### The Problem\nThree charges are arranged in an equilateral triangle with side $a \u003d 15\\text{ cm}$.\n*   **Bottom Left ($q_1$):** $1\\ \\mu\\text{As}$\n*   **Bottom Right ($q_2$):** $1\\ \\mu\\text{As}$\n*   **Top ($q_3$):** $2q_1 \u003d 2\\ \\mu\\text{As}$\nA small charge ($q \u003d 2 \\times 10^{-8}\\text{ As}$, $m \u003d 3\\text{ g}$) is placed exactly in the **centroid** (težišče) of the triangle.\n*   **a)** What is the initial acceleration of the small charge when released?\n*   **b)** What is its velocity when it crosses the line connecting $q_1$ and $q_2$ (the bottom base)?\n\n---\n\n### Part 1: The Logic for Acceleration (Part A)\nAcceleration comes from the net force ($F \u003d ma$). Since all the charges are positive, the small charge $q$ is repelled by all three corners.\n*   $q_1$ pushes it up and to the right.\n*   $q_2$ pushes it up and to the left.\n*   $q_3$ pushes it straight down.\nBecause $q_1$ and $q_2$ are equal charges and symmetrically placed, their **horizontal forces perfectly cancel each other out**. They work together to push the charge straight up.\nMeanwhile, the top charge $q_3$ is twice as strong ($2q_1$) and pushes straight down. We just need to subtract the upward pull of $1$ and $2$ from the downward push of $3$ to find the net force!\n\n### Part 2: The Logic for Velocity (Part B)\nJust like in problems 4 and 6, the force changes as the particle moves downwards. We **cannot use kinematics** to find the final speed; we must use **Conservation of Energy**.\n*   We need the total Electric Potential ($V$) at the **start point** (the centroid).\n*   We need the total Electric Potential ($V$) at the **end point** (the exact midpoint between $q_1$ and $q_2$).\n*   The loss in potential energy turns into kinetic energy.\n\n---\n\n### Part 3: The Formulas to Recall\n\n**1. Geometry of an Equilateral Triangle:**\n*   Distance from a corner to the centroid: $r \u003d \\frac{a}{\\sqrt{3}}$\n*   Height of the triangle (from base to top corner): $h \u003d \\frac{a\\sqrt{3}}{2}$\n\n**2. Coulomb\u0027s Law \u0026 Force Vectors:**\n$$F \u003d \\frac{1}{4\\pi\\epsilon_0} \\frac{Q q}{r^2}$$\n*To get the vertical (upward) part of the force from the bottom corners, you must multiply the force by $\\cos(60^\\circ) \u003d 0.5$ due to the angles in the triangle.*\n\n**3. Electric Potential ($V$):**\n$$V_{total} \u003d \\frac{1}{4\\pi\\epsilon_0} \\left( \\frac{q_1}{r_1} + \\frac{q_2}{r_2} + \\frac{q_3}{r_3} \\right)$$\n\n**4. Conservation of Energy:**\n$$\\frac{1}{2}mv^2 \u003d q \\cdot (V_{start} - V_{end})$$\n\n---\n\n### Part 4: How to solve it (Putting it together)\n\n#### Step 1: Solve for Acceleration (Part a)\nThe distance from the corners to the centroid is $r \u003d \\frac{0.15}{\\sqrt{3}} \\approx 0.0866\\text{ m}$.\n*   **Downward force from $q_3$:** \n    $$F_{down} \u003d \\frac{1}{4\\pi\\epsilon_0} \\frac{q_3 \\cdot q}{r^2}$$\n*   **Upward force from $q_1$ and $q_2$:**\n    Each pushes up with $F_y \u003d F \\cdot \\cos(60^\\circ) \u003d F \\cdot 0.5$. Since there are two of them, the total upward force is just $2 \\cdot (F \\cdot 0.5) \u003d F$.\n    $$F_{up} \u003d \\frac{1}{4\\pi\\epsilon_0} \\frac{q_1 \\cdot q}{r^2}$$\n*   **Net Force:**\n    Since $q_3 \u003d 2q_1$, the downward force is exactly twice as big as the upward force.\n    $$F_{net} \u003d F_{down} - F_{up} \u003d \\frac{1}{4\\pi\\epsilon_0} \\frac{q_1 \\cdot q}{r^2}$$\n*   **Acceleration:** Use $a_{acc} \u003d \\frac{F_{net}}{m}$. \n    *(Plug in $q_1\u003d10^{-6}\\text{ C}$, $q\u003d2\\times 10^{-8}\\text{ C}$, $r^2\u003d0.0075\\text{ m}^2$, $m\u003d0.003\\text{ kg}$. You will get exactly **$a_{acc} \u003d 8.0\\text{ m/s}^2$**!)*\n\n#### Step 2: Solve for Potentials (Part b)\n**At the Start (Centroid):**\nThe distance to all three charges is $r \\approx 0.0866\\text{ m}$.\n$$V_{start} \u003d \\frac{1}{4\\pi\\epsilon_0} \\left( \\frac{q_1}{r} + \\frac{q_2}{r} + \\frac{q_3}{r} \\right) \u003d \\frac{1}{4\\pi\\epsilon_0} \\left( \\frac{4 \\cdot q_1}{r} \\right)$$\n*(If you calculate this, $V_{start} \\approx 415,692\\text{ V}$)*\n\n**At the End (Midpoint of the base):**\nIt is now sitting exactly between $q_1$ and $q_2$, so it is distance $\\frac{a}{2} \u003d 0.075\\text{ m}$ away from them.\nIt is distance $h \u003d \\frac{a\\sqrt{3}}{2} \\approx 0.1299\\text{ m}$ away from the top charge $q_3$.\n$$V_{end} \u003d \\frac{1}{4\\pi\\epsilon_0} \\left( \\frac{q_1}{0.075} + \\frac{q_2}{0.075} + \\frac{q_3}{0.1299} \\right)$$\n*(If you calculate this, $V_{end} \\approx 378,564\\text{ V}$)*\n\n#### Step 3: Solve for Velocity\nUse the energy conservation equation:\n$$\\frac{1}{2} m v^2 \u003d q \\cdot (V_{start} - V_{end})$$\n$$v \u003d \\sqrt{ \\frac{2 \\cdot q \\cdot (V_{start} - V_{end})}{m} }$$\n*(Plug in your values: $\\Delta V \\approx 37,128\\text{ V}$, $m \u003d 0.003\\text{ kg}$, $q \u003d 2\\times 10^{-8}\\text{ C}$. You will get **$v \\approx 0.703\\text{ m/s}$**, which matches the solution!)*",

      "text": "\n\n\nHere is the step-by-step logic and the formulas you need for the **eighth problem** (the first one under the \"Maribor, 18. aprila 2003\" banner, involving the spherical shell and the small sphere shot through a hole).\n\nThis problem introduces a very important electrostatic concept: **the electric field and potential inside a hollow shell** (which was covered on Slide 10 of your FIZIKA II.pdf).\n\n### The Problem\nA thin spherical shell ($R \u003d 10\\text{ cm}$) has a uniform positive charge ($q_0 \u003d +10\\ \\mu\\text{As}$). We place a small positive charge ($q \u003d +0.5\\ \\mu\\text{As}$, $m \u003d 1\\text{ g}$) in the exact center and shoot it outward with an initial velocity $v_0 \u003d 30\\text{ m/s}$. It escapes through a tiny hole.\n*   **a)** What is its velocity when it is $x \u003d 40\\text{ cm}$ away from the shell?\n*   **b)** What is its terminal (final) velocity ($v_{kon}$)?\n\n---\n\n### Part 1: The Logic (What happens physically?)\n1. **Inside the Shell:** According to the **Shell Theorem (Izrek za krogelne lupine)**, the electric field *inside* a uniformly charged spherical shell is exactly **zero** ($E \u003d 0$). \n   * Because there is no electric field inside, there is no electric force! \n   * This means the small sphere coasts from the center to the hole at a perfectly constant speed of $v_0 \u003d 30\\text{ m/s}$.\n   * Since $E \u003d 0$, the Electric Potential ($V$) inside the shell doesn\u0027t change; it is constant everywhere inside and equals the potential at the surface.\n2. **Outside the Shell:** As soon as the small sphere exits the hole, it enters the electric field of the shell. Since both charges are positive, the shell violently repels the small sphere, accelerating it forward.\n3. **The Math Approach:** Just like the previous problems, because the force weakens as the particle gets further away, we cannot use $F\u003dma$. We must use **Conservation of Energy**. \n\n---\n\n### Part 2: The Formulas to Recall\n\n**1. Electric Potential ($V$) of a Spherical Shell:**\n*   **Inside and on the surface ($r \\le R$):** $V_{inside} \u003d \\frac{1}{4\\pi\\epsilon_0} \\frac{q_0}{R}$\n*   **Outside ($r \u003e R$):** $V_{outside} \u003d \\frac{1}{4\\pi\\epsilon_0} \\frac{q_0}{r}$\n*(Note that for the outside, $r$ is the distance from the **center** of the sphere, not the surface!)*\n\n**2. You are thinking exactly like a physicist. \n\nBefore you can just \"know\" the formula for Electric Potential ($V$), you formally have to find the Electric Field ($\\vec{E}$) everywhere in space. And to find $\\vec{E}$, you start from the very foundation: the continuous charge integral you just mentioned (which is exactly on **Slide 13** of your lectures):\n\n$$ \\vec{E}(\\vec{r}) \u003d \\frac{1}{4\\pi\\epsilon_0} \\int \\frac{\\vec{r} - \\vec{r}\u0027}{|\\vec{r} - \\vec{r}\u0027|^3} dq $$\n\nIf you wanted to do this the \"brute force\" way, you would slice the spherical shell into tiny rings, set $dq \u003d \\sigma \\, dS$, and integrate over the entire surface of the sphere. The horizontal components of the vectors would cancel out due to symmetry, and after doing some slightly nasty calculus, you would get exactly the **Shell Theorem (Izrek za krogelne lupine, Slide 10)**.\n\nHowever, your professor gives you a massive \"cheat code\" to avoid doing that nasty integral: **Gauss\u0027s Law (Gaussov zakon, Slide 19)!**\n\nHere is the exact pipeline of how you would formally derive the formulas we used:\n\n### Step 1: Use Gauss\u0027s Law to find $\\vec{E}$\nInstead of integrating over every $dq$, you draw an imaginary \"Gaussian sphere\" of radius $r$ and use the law: $\\oint \\vec{E} \\cdot d\\vec{S} \u003d \\frac{q_{enc}}{\\epsilon_0}$\n\n*   **Inside the shell ($r \u003c R$):** The imaginary sphere inside the shell encloses *no charge* ($q_{enc} \u003d 0$). Therefore, $\\vec{E} \u003d 0$.\n*   **Outside the shell ($r \u003e R$):** The imaginary sphere encloses the whole shell ($q_{enc} \u003d q_0$). The surface area of your imaginary sphere is $4\\pi r^2$.\n    $$ E \\cdot (4\\pi r^2) \u003d \\frac{q_0}{\\epsilon_0} \\implies E \u003d \\frac{1}{4\\pi\\epsilon_0}\\frac{q_0}{r^2} $$\n\n### Step 2: Integrate $\\vec{E}$ to find Potential $V$\nOnce you have the Electric Field, you use the definition of potential from **Slide 22**: \n$$ V \u003d -\\int \\vec{E} \\cdot d\\vec{r} $$\n\n*   **Outside:** If you integrate $\\frac{1}{r^2} dr$, you get $-\\frac{1}{r}$. The negatives cancel, leaving you with $V \u003d \\frac{1}{4\\pi\\epsilon_0}\\frac{q_0}{r}$.\n*   **Inside:** Because $E \u003d 0$ inside, the integral is zero, meaning the potential *does not change* from whatever it was at the surface. So inside, $V$ is a constant value of $\\frac{1}{4\\pi\\epsilon_0}\\frac{q_0}{R}$.\n\n### Step 3: Use $V$ to find Energy\nNow you multiply the potential by the small charge $q$ to get Potential Energy ($U \u003d qV$), which is where we started in Part 1 of the solution!\n\nIt is fantastic that you caught this. While you probably won\u0027t have to do the full $dq$ integral for a sphere on the exam (since Gauss\u0027s law is expected), knowing *why* the field drops to zero inside and how the integral builds the field proves you really understand the mechanics of Electrostatics!",

      "text": "\n\n\nI believe we actually just covered the 8th problem (the spherical shell with the small charge shot through the hole) in the last couple of messages! \n\nI\u0027ll assume you lost count and meant the **9th problem** (the one with the capacitor, switch, and Wheatstone bridge). If you really did want to review the 8th one again, just let me know!\n\nHere is the step-by-step logic and the formulas you need for the **ninth problem**. This is a great problem because it transitions us from Electrostatics into **Electric Circuits**.\n\n### The Problem\nA capacitor ($C$) is connected in series with two unknown resistors ($R_1$ and $R_2$). The capacitor is charged to $U_0 \u003d 200\\text{ V}$. We close the switch, and in $t \u003d 3\\text{ ms}$, the voltage drops to $U_1 \u003d 50\\text{ V}$.\nWe measure the resistors using a Wheatstone bridge with a known resistor $R \u003d 100\\ \\Omega$ and a $l\u003d1\\text{ m}$ ($100\\text{ cm}$) long wire. The galvanometer reads zero when the slider is at $x_1 \u003d 35\\text{ cm}$ for $R_1$, and at $x_2 \u003d 60\\text{ cm}$ for $R_2$. What is $C$?\n\n---\n\n### Part 1: The Logic (The Wheatstone Bridge)\n1. **What is it?** A Wheatstone bridge (diagram \u0027b\u0027) is a clever circuit used to measure unknown resistances. It splits the current into a top branch (with the resistors) and a bottom branch (the slide-wire).\n2. **The \"Balanced\" State:** The galvanometer (G) connects the two branches. When it reads exactly zero current, the bridge is \"balanced.\" This means the electrical potential at the top junction is perfectly equal to the potential at the slider on the bottom wire.\n3. **The Ratio:** Because the voltages match, the ratio of the top two resistors must perfectly equal the ratio of the wire lengths on the bottom. \n\n### Part 2: The Logic (The RC Circuit)\n1. **The Setup:** In diagram \u0027a\u0027, the capacitor and the two resistors form a simple closed loop when the switch is flipped.\n2. **Discharging:** The capacitor acts like a temporary battery. As it pushes current through the resistors, it loses its stored charge, and its voltage drops.\n3. **Exponential Decay:** The voltage doesn\u0027t drop linearly; it drops exponentially. The speed at which it drains is controlled by the \"Time Constant\" ($\\tau \u003d R_{eq} \\cdot C$). A higher resistance or a higher capacitance means it drains slower.\n\n---\n\n### Part 3: The Formulas to Recall\n\n**1. Wheatstone Bridge (Balanced):**\n$$\\frac{R_{unknown}}{R_{known}} \u003d \\frac{x}{l - x}$$\n*(Where $x$ is the left side of the wire, and $l-x$ is the rest of the wire).*\n\n**2. Series Resistors:**\n$$R_{eq} \u003d R_1 + R_2$$\n\n**3. Capacitor Discharging:**\n(From FIZIKA II slide 43: *Praznjenje kondenzatorja*)\n$$U(t) \u003d U_0 e^{-\\frac{t}{\\tau}}$$\n*(Where $\\tau \u003d R_{eq} \\cdot C$)*\n\n---\n\n### Part 4: How to solve it (Putting it together)\n\n**Step 1: Find $R_1$**\nUse the Wheatstone formula for $x_1 \u003d 35\\text{ cm}$ and total length $l \u003d 100\\text{ cm}$:\n$$R_1 \u003d R \\cdot \\frac{x_1}{100 - x_1}$$\n$$R_1 \u003d 100 \\cdot \\frac{35}{65} \\approx \\mathbf{53.85\\ \\Omega}$$\n\n**Step 2: Find $R_2$**\nUse the formula for $x_2 \u003d 60\\text{ cm}$:\n$$R_2 \u003d 100 \\cdot \\frac{60}{100 - 60} \u003d 100 \\cdot \\frac{60}{40} \u003d \\mathbf{150\\ \\Omega}$$\n\n**Step 3: Total Resistance in the RC Circuit**\nBecause they are connected in series in diagram \u0027a\u0027:\n$$R_{eq} \u003d R_1 + R_2 \u003d 53.85 + 150 \u003d \\mathbf{203.85\\ \\Omega}$$\n\n**Step 4: Solve for Capacitance ($C$)**\nStart with the exponential discharge formula:\n$$U_1 \u003d U_0 e^{-\\frac{t}{R_{eq} \\cdot C}}$$\nDivide by $U_0$:\n$$\\frac{50}{200} \u003d e^{-\\frac{0.003}{203.85 \\cdot C}}$$\n$$0.25 \u003d e^{-\\frac{0.003}{203.85 \\cdot C}}$$\nTo get rid of the exponential \"$e$\", take the natural log ($\\ln$) of both sides:\n$$\\ln(0.25) \u003d -\\frac{0.003}{203.85 \\cdot C}$$\nIsolate $C$:\n$$C \u003d \\frac{-0.003}{203.85 \\cdot \\ln(0.25)}$$\n\n*(If you type this into your calculator, remember that $\\ln(0.25) \\approx -1.386$. The negative signs will cancel out nicely. You will get exactly $C \u003d 1.061 \\times 10^{-5}\\text{ F}$, which is exactly **$10.6\\ \\mu\\text{F}$**!)*",

      "text": "\n\n\nHere is the step-by-step logic and the formulas you need for the **10th problem** (the complex circuit diagram at the bottom of Page 2).\n\nThis is a fantastic problem that tests your ability to use **Kirchhoff\u0027s Laws (Nodal Analysis)** and understand how **Capacitors** behave in DC circuits over time.\n\n### Part 1: Deciphering the Circuit Topology\nBefore calculating anything, we must understand how the circuit is wired. It consists of three parallel branches connected to a top wire (let\u0027s call it **Node A**) and a bottom wire (let\u0027s call it **Node B**, which we will set to $0\\text{ V}$ like a ground).\n*   **Middle Branch:** Contains internal resistance $R_{n1} \u003d 10\\ \\Omega$ and battery $U_{g1} \u003d 6\\text{ V}$. The long line of the battery is on top, meaning it pushes $+6\\text{ V}$ towards Node A.\n*   **Right Branch:** Contains $R_1$, $R_{n2}$, battery $U_{g2}$, and $R_5$. These are all in series on this branch. \n    *   Total resistance: $R_{right} \u003d R_1 + R_{n2} + R_5 \u003d 20 + 7 + 60 \u003d \\mathbf{87\\ \\Omega}$.\n    *   The battery $U_{g2} \u003d 4.5\\text{ V}$ also has its long line on top, pushing $+4.5\\text{ V}$ towards Node A.\n*   **Left Branch:** Contains $R_2 \u003d 80\\ \\Omega$ at the top, $R_4 \u003d 40\\ \\Omega$ at the bottom, and the Switch $S$ in the middle. \n    *   **Position 1** connects the circuit through resistor $R_3 \u003d 100\\ \\Omega$.\n    *   **Position 2** connects the circuit through the capacitor $C \u003d 50\\ \\mu\\text{F}$ (replacing $R_3$).\n\nWe will solve this using **Nodal Analysis (Kirchhoff\u0027s Current Law)** at Node A: *The sum of all currents leaving Node A must equal zero.*\n\n---\n\n### Part A: Switch in Position 1\n**The Logic:**\nWhen the switch is in Position 1, the current flows through $R_3$ and completely bypasses the capacitor. The left branch is just three resistors in series.\n*   $R_{left} \u003d R_2 + R_3 + R_4 \u003d 80 + 100 + 40 \u003d \\mathbf{220\\ \\Omega}$.\n\n**The Calculation:**\nSet up Kirchhoff\u0027s Current Law for Node A:\n$$I_{left} + I_{middle} + I_{right} \u003d 0$$\n$$\\frac{V_A - 0}{220} + \\frac{V_A - 6}{10} + \\frac{V_A - 4.5}{87} \u003d 0$$\nSeparate the fractions:\n$$V_A \\left(\\frac{1}{220} + \\frac{1}{10} + \\frac{1}{87}\\right) \u003d \\frac{6}{10} + \\frac{4.5}{87}$$\n$$V_A (0.004545 + 0.1 + 0.011494) \u003d 0.6 + 0.051724$$\n$$V_A (0.11604) \u003d 0.651724 \\implies \\mathbf{V_A \u003d 5.616\\text{ V}}$$\n\nThe question asks for the current through $R_5$, which is the current flowing down the entire right branch ($I_{right}$):\n$$I_5 \u003d \\frac{V_A - 4.5}{87} \u003d \\frac{5.616 - 4.5}{87} \u003d \\frac{1.116}{87} \u003d \\mathbf{0.0128\\text{ A}} \\text{ (or } \\mathbf{12.8\\text{ mA}})$$\n\n---\n\n### Part B: Immediately after switching to Position 2\n**The Logic:**\nWe flip the switch to Position 2. The left branch now contains $R_2$, $C$, and $R_4$. \nAt the exact instant we flip the switch ($t \u003d 0^+$), the capacitor is completely empty. **An uncharged capacitor acts exactly like a plain wire (a short circuit, $0\\ \\Omega$)**. \n*   Therefore, for this split second, the left branch\u0027s resistance drops because $R_3$ is gone and $C$ has no resistance yet!\n*   $R_{left} \u003d R_2 + 0 + R_4 \u003d 80 + 40 \u003d \\mathbf{120\\ \\Omega}$.\n\n**The Calculation:**\nSet up the KCL equation again, just changing the left denominator:\n$$\\frac{V_A - 0}{120} + \\frac{V_A - 6}{10} + \\frac{V_A - 4.5}{87} \u003d 0$$\n$$V_A \\left(\\frac{1}{120} + \\frac{1}{10} + \\frac{1}{87}\\right) \u003d \\frac{6}{10} + \\frac{4.5}{87}$$\n$$V_A (0.008333 + 0.1 + 0.011494) \u003d 0.651724$$\n$$V_A (0.119827) \u003d 0.651724 \\implies \\mathbf{V_A \u003d 5.439\\text{ V}}$$\n\nCalculate the new current through the right branch ($I_5$):\n$$I_5 \u003d \\frac{V_A - 4.5}{87} \u003d \\frac{5.439 - 4.5}{87} \u003d \\frac{0.939}{87} \u003d \\mathbf{0.0108\\text{ A}} \\text{ (or } \\mathbf{10.8\\text{ mA}})$$\n\n---\n\n### Part C: A long time after switching to Position 2\n**The Logic:**\nIf we leave the switch in Position 2 for a long time ($t \\to \\infty$), the capacitor completely fills up with charge. **A fully charged capacitor acts like an open circuit (infinite resistance)**. \n*   This means NO current can flow through the left branch anymore ($I_{left} \u003d 0$).\n*   Because no current flows through the left branch, there is **zero voltage drop** across resistors $R_2$ and $R_4$. Therefore, the entire voltage difference between Node A and Node B ($V_A - 0$) is sitting directly across the capacitor!\n\n**The Calculation:**\nSet up KCL again, but completely remove the left branch:\n$$\\frac{V_A - 6}{10} + \\frac{V_A - 4.5}{87} \u003d 0$$\nMultiply the whole equation by $870$ (or cross-multiply) to solve for $V_A$:\n$$87(V_A - 6) + 10(V_A - 4.5) \u003d 0$$\n$$87V_A - 522 + 10V_A - 45 \u003d 0$$\n$$97V_A \u003d 567 \\implies \\mathbf{V_A \u003d 5.845\\text{ V}}$$\n\nSince the full voltage $V_A$ rests across the capacitor, $U_C \u003d 5.845\\text{ V}$.\nFinally, calculate the stored charge using the capacitor formula ($q \u003d C \\cdot U$):\n$$q_C \u003d 50\\ \\mu\\text{F} \\cdot 5.845\\text{ V}$$\n$$q_C \u003d 50 \\times 10^{-6} \\cdot 5.845 \u003d \\mathbf{292.25 \\times 10^{-6}\\text{ As}}$$\nWhich perfectly rounds to **$292\\ \\mu\\text{As}$**!",
